lead: A data transfer instruction copies a byte or a word from one place to another: register to register, memory to register, register to memory, or an I/O port to the accumulator. It does not add, subtract or compare. It exists because the ALU can only work on values already in registers, so data must be moved there first. Every program uses these instructions: reading a sensor port, loading a constant from a look-up table, saving a result back to memory. The source is not erased; only the destination changes.
prereq: You need: 3.2 Addressing modes and the register models from Unit 2, 8085 and 8086 Microprocessors.

blocks.text: The instruction writes a destination and reads a source. After MOV A,B both A and B hold the same byte, because B is copied and not consumed. This is why the operation is called a transfer even though nothing leaves the source.

On the 8085 the destination is written first. MOV r1,r2 copies register r2 into register r1. MVI r,data copies an 8-bit constant into r. The symbol M means the memory byte whose address is in HL, so MOV M,r writes memory and MOV r,M reads it. A memory access is slower than a register copy because it drives the address and data buses (see Unit 2, Timing diagrams and machine cycles).

Most transfers leave the flags alone. The 8085 MOV, MVI, LDA, STA, LDAX, STAX, LHLD, SHLD, XCHG, IN and OUT do not touch the five flags (S, Z, AC, P, CY). The 8086 MOV, XCHG, LEA, LDS, LES, XLAT, IN and OUT do not touch them either. A copy is not an arithmetic result: a zero byte copied is not an arithmetic zero, and the CPU must not let a later jump change because of a move. Instructions that load a flag register on purpose are the exception, and their names say so.
Two rules follow. Never expect a move to set or clear a flag. Never expect the source to be erased.

Action
rows: A ← [rp], rp is BC or DE

blocks.text: LHLD and SHLD use 16-bit addresses and store the low byte first: the byte at addr16 goes to L, the byte at addr16+1 goes to H. Reading the pair the other way is the classic byte-order mistake.

LDAX and STAX exist only for BC and DE. There is no LDAX H or STAX H opcode, and none is needed, since MOV A,M and MOV M,A already copy between A and the byte at HL. XCHG swaps HL and DE in one instruction, so 16-bit arithmetic on HL can continue on the other pair; it changes no flags, so a carry from an earlier operation survives the swap.

IN and OUT carry an 8-bit port address inside the instruction, and the accumulator is the only register that can talk to a port. Some syllabi group IN and OUT under data transfer, others under I/O; the operation is still a copy between A and a port latch.

8086. MOV copies a byte or word between registers, between a register and memory, or between a segment register and a register or memory. Memory-to-memory MOV does not exist; one operand must be a register. XCHG swaps two operands, at least one in a register. LEA loads the effective address, not the contents: with SI = 0100H, LEA BX,[SI+4] puts 0104H in BX, while MOV BX,[SI+4] would load the two bytes stored at 0104H. LDS and LES load a far pointer: a 16-bit offset into the named register and a 16-bit segment into DS or ES. XLAT replaces AL with the byte at BX+AL, a one-instruction table look-up. IN and OUT take a 16-bit port address from DX or an 8-bit address from the instruction.

8051. MOV works inside the chip: registers, internal RAM, special function registers and single bits. MOVX moves A to or from external data memory through DPTR or R0/R1. MOVC reads program memory, used for constants. XCHD swaps the low nibble of A with the low nibble of an internal RAM byte and leaves both high nibbles alone. SWAP A exchanges the two nibbles of A. PUSH and POP copy through the stack and change SP each time; the details are in 3.6 Stack and subroutines.
None of these change flags. PUSH and POP are not plain copies: they move the stack pointer, so a loop that pushes without popping will overflow the stack area.

examples.question: An 8085 system has A = 25H, B = 4AH, HL = 2050H, and memory [2050H] = FFH. Execute MOV A,B and then MOV M,A. Give A, B and [2050H] after both instructions, and say what happens to the flags.
steps: Write the starting state: A = 25H = 37, B = 4AH = 74, HL = 2050H, [2050H] = FFH = 255.
MOV A,B reads B and writes A. A becomes 4AH = 74. B keeps 4AH = 74. Memory is untouched at FFH.
MOV M,A uses M = [HL] = [2050H]. A is 4AH, so [2050H] becomes 4AH = 74. A stays 4AH and B stays 4AH.
MOV does not touch flags, so S, Z, AC, P and CY keep their earlier values.
examples.answer: A = 4AH = 74, B = 4AH = 74, and [2050H] = 4AH = 74; the flags are unchanged.
examples.check:
a = 0x25
b = 0x4A
mem = 0xFF
a = b
mem = a
print(a)
print(b)
print(mem)

traps: MOV A,B changes A only; B is not cleared, so both registers end with the same byte.
MOV M,r writes memory at HL, while MOV r,M reads memory at HL. The position of M matters.
LDAX and STAX exist only for BC and DE. There is no LDAX H or STAX H opcode, and none is needed; MOV A,M and MOV M,A already copy between A and the byte at HL.
LEA gives the address and MOV gives the contents. LEA BX,[SI] and MOV BX,[SI] give very different values.
PUSH and POP change SP, so they are not simple copies; an unmatched PUSH in a loop overflows the stack.

quiz.q: What does MOV A,B do on the 8085?
quiz.a: It copies the byte in B into A. B keeps its value, and no flag changes.

quiz.q: Why does the 8085 have both MOV and MVI?
quiz.a: MOV copies from a register or from memory at HL; MVI copies an 8-bit constant that is part of the instruction. The source of the byte is different.

quiz.q: A = 3FH, HL = 2100H, and [2100H] = 88H. After MOV M,A followed by MOV A,M, give A and [2100H].
quiz.a: MOV M,A writes 3FH to [2100H], so memory becomes 3FH. MOV A,M then reads it back into A, so A = 3FH and [2100H] = 3FH.

quiz.q: 8086: SI = 0100H, [0104H] = 1234H. Give BX after LEA BX,[SI+4] and AX after MOV AX,[SI+4].
quiz.a: SI+4 = 0104H. LEA loads the address, so BX = 0104H. MOV loads the contents, so AX = 1234H.

quiz.q: Why is there no MOV M,M on the 8085?
quiz.a: The opcode that would encode it, 76H, is used for HLT, and a memory-to-memory copy would need two memory accesses, one read and one write, in the same instruction, so the encoding was not offered.

quiz.q: Give two reasons XCHG is preferred over an equivalent MOV sequence for swapping HL and DE in an 8085 program.
quiz.a: XCHG takes one byte and one instruction. An equivalent MOV sequence needs six MOV instructions and six bytes: MOV A,H, MOV H,D, MOV D,A, MOV A,L, MOV L,E, MOV E,A. So XCHG saves five bytes and five instructions. The MOV sequence must use A as a temporary and destroys its old value; XCHG swaps HL and DE without using A, so A, B, C and the flags keep their values (only H, L, D and E are exchanged).

quiz.q: State one difference between MOVX and MOVC on the 8051.
quiz.a: MOVX reads or writes external data memory using DPTR or R0/R1. MOVC reads program memory, typically a constant table, using A+DPTR or A+PC. Both move data through A.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern RISC designs split transfers into load and store instructions, and the ARM load-store group in Unit 6 follows that pattern. Compilers of embedded C spend much of their effort allocating variables to registers so that the transfer count drops. DMA controllers, covered with the 8257 in Unit 5, take over block copies so the CPU does not execute a transfer per byte. Searching for load-store architecture, register allocation and direct memory access will take you further into this idea.
